summary: Creates a registry of Authentication Method Reference values and defines an initial set. These values go in the amr claim of JSON Web Tokens to say how a user was authenticated, for example by password or one-time code.

plainLanguage.summary: When you get a wristband, it can note how you proved who you were, like showing a card. This is the list of words for that.

questions: how to register an amr value
subtitle: A shared vocabulary and registry for saying how a user proved who they are inside a JSON Web Token.

tldr.problem: The "amr" claim lets an identity provider say which authentication methods were used, but no standard values for it existed, so parties had to agree on meanings privately.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8176 creates an IANA registry of Authentication Method Reference values and registers an initial set of short names such as pwd, otp, fpt and mfa.
tldr.outcome: Identity providers and relying parties can use the same short identifiers, and other specifications can add more values through Expert Review.

facts.label: Escalation to IESG
facts.value: Requests undetermined for longer than 21 days

today: RFC 8176 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the initial contents of the IANA Authentication Method Reference Values registry, to which other specifications can add values.

sections.title: The Problem: Unnamed Authentication Methods
sections.content:
The amr (Authentication Methods References) claim is defined by OpenID Connect Core 1.0 and registered in the IANA "JSON Web Token Claims" registry. It is an optional JSON array of case-sensitive strings that name the authentication methods used, for example that both a password and a one-time password were used.

OpenID Connect leaves the actual values out of scope and says the parties using the claim must agree on what they mean. RFC 8176 fills that gap by creating a registry of values and defining an initial set.

The RFC also warns that the existence of amr should not be read as encouragement to use OAuth 2.0 for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is built for authorization and needs extensions, such as OpenID Connect, to authenticate securely.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can tell another site how you logged in, but there was no common list of words for it. This RFC writes that list.

sections.title: Design Principles for the Values
sections.content:
Each value usually names a family of closely related methods. The otp value covers one-time passwords based on both time and HMAC, because many relying parties only care that a one-time password was used in addition to a password. The fpt value likewise covers fingerprint matching without separating every sensor or matching algorithm.

The initial set is intentionally small and limited to values already used in practice. The RFC argues that slicing methods more finely than relying parties actually would hurt interoperability, because they would have to learn that many values mean the same thing to them.

Trust still rests on the identity provider. The amr value only lets it signal extra information about what it did, for the cases where that helps the relying party.
sections.plainLanguage: The words are broad on purpose, like saying "fruit" instead of naming every kind of apple. Most people just need to know it was a fruit.

sections.title: The Defined Values
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC defines the initial values. They fall into a few groups.

  • Biometrics: face (facial recognition), fpt (fingerprint), iris (iris scan), retina (retina scan) and vbm (voiceprint).
  • Secrets and keys: pwd (password), pin (a PIN or pattern used to unlock a key on the device), otp (one-time password), hwk and swk (proof of possession of a hardware-secured or software-secured key) and sc (smart card).
  • Out-of-band confirmation: sms (text message to a registered number) and tel (telephone call to a registered number).
  • Combinations and context: mfa (multiple-factor), mca (multiple-channel), kba (knowledge-based), rba (risk-based), geo (geolocation), user (user presence test) and wia (Windows integrated authentication).

When mfa is present, the specific methods used may also be listed.
sections.plainLanguage: The list has short labels for ways to prove who you are: a secret word, a code sent to your phone, or your fingerprint or face.

sections.title: How amr Differs from acr
sections.content:
The acr (Authentication Context Class Reference) claim is related but different. An Authentication Context Class is a set of business rules that an authentication is asked to satisfy, and many different methods, alone or combined, can satisfy it. The acr reply says the rules were met, not how.

The amr claim instead states which particular methods were used. The RFC notes this tends to be more brittle, because the methods suited to a given authentication change over time as attacks on existing methods evolve and new methods are deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: acr says "you passed the test". amr says exactly which tools you used to pass it.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The list of amr values in an ID Token reveals how the user authenticated, and in some cases that may have privacy implications. The RFC defines identifiers only. It does not say how credentials are stored or protected, and securing the biometric credentials behind some values is out of scope.

For security, the considerations in OpenID Connect Core 1.0, RFC 6749 and the entire OAuth 2.0 Threat Model (RFC 6819) apply. Depending on particular authentication methods may also make systems brittle, as described for acr comparison above.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling someone how you got in can reveal things about you. The list only names the methods and does not say how to keep them safe.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
The RFC establishes the IANA "Authentication Method Reference Values" registry. Each entry records the value and a reference to the specification that defines it. New values are added by Expert Review after a three-week review period on the jwt-reg-review mailing list. Requests left undetermined for longer than 21 days can be brought to the IESG.

The registration template asks for a name, a description, a change controller and specification documents. It is RECOMMENDED that the name not exceed 8 characters without a compelling reason. Names are case sensitive, use only printable ASCII excluding double quote and backslash, and may not match another registered name when compared case-insensitively unless the Designated Experts state a compelling reason. For Standards Track RFCs the change controller is IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: New words go through a short review by a few experts, like a club checking a new rule before adding it to the rulebook.
